plan: [With three bidders the winner pays the third‑highest bid — i.e., the minimum of the three bids. My bid mostly only affects whether I win, not the price I pay. To maximize long‑run profit I should bid aggressively to win whenever at least one opponent is cheap. There is no history to exploit this round, and my value is $30, so I bid the maximum allowed to maximize expected surplus.]

[Three-bidder third-price: the winner pays the lowest (third) bid, so my own bid only affects winning probability. Assume symmetric strategy s(v)=c v; solving the first-order condition yields c=2. Thus the Bayes–Nash equilibrium bidding function is s(v)=2v. With value $35 the equilibrium bid is 2*35=$70, which maximizes long-run expected profit under uniform [0,49].]

[Assume other bidders report their values (no history). For third-price with three bidders, your bid affects only the chance to win; expected profit (assuming others bid truthfully) is maximized at b = 2v. With v = $6, set b = $12. This balances win probability vs. expected payment (expected minimum of others conditional on winning = b/3). Bid in $0.1 increments: $12.0.]
